html:
The Battle of Trenton was fought on the morning of 26 December 1776 at Trenton, New Jersey, in today's United States. George Washington's army crossed the Delaware River by night and captured a garrison of Hessians, German soldiers hired by Britain.

The first months of the American Revolutionary War after independence had gone badly. Washington had lost New York and been chased across New Jersey. His army was down to a few thousand men, and most of their service ended on 31 December. He needed a win. On Christmas night he took about 2,400 men across the icy river in boats, through a storm of snow and sleet, and marched 14 km to Trenton. The attack began about eight in the morning. The 1,500 Hessians were caught off guard and their commander, Colonel Rall, was fatally wounded. About 900 were captured. Only a handful of Americans were hurt.

A week later Washington won again at Princeton, and the British pulled back from most of New Jersey. Trenton was a small battle with a large effect. It restored belief in the cause, men signed on again, and the army of the new United States lived to fight on.
